headline: White Island Still Holding Cod While Hampton's Back Channels Fill With Snapper Blues
subhead: Thirteen miles of coastline is plenty if you fish it like it's a hundred and thirty — the Shoals proved that again this week.
body_markdown:
People hear thirteen miles of coastline and figure there's nothing to write about. I've never understood that. Thirteen miles gets you the Piscataqua pushing out past Portsmouth Harbor, it gets you the Isles of Shoals sitting nine miles offshore in real groundfish water, and it gets you Hampton Harbor filling and draining twice a day with enough current to make a tide chart necessary reading. I trailer a twenty-foot Lund out of Rye Harbor most mornings and I fish this stretch like it's Jeffreys Ledge on a bad day and the Grand Banks on a good one. This week was more the former than the latter, but that's not the same as a bad week.

Cod are still stacked on the ledges around White Island and Duck Island, same pattern we've had since mid-July — nothing dramatic, just steady. I've been anchoring up on the northeast corner of White Island in 60 to 80 feet, letting the boat settle on the last of the ebb, and jigging diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid straight down. Slack tide through the first hour of the flood has been the window — anything with real current running and the fish just aren't holding position the same way. Cod are running 3 to 6 pounds mostly, with the occasional fish pushing 8 that makes the trip worth the diesel. Haddock have been mixed in but thin — you'll pick off one or two on a good drift over the gravel patches southeast of Appledore, but I wouldn't plan a trip around them right now. Water out there is still holding in that classic low-60s Gulf of Maine range, which keeps everything honest and slow-moving rather than blown out or bait-starved. We said a couple weeks back this zone would stay in its typical mid-August pattern rather than showing any of the warm-water excitement building to the south, and that's exactly what's held — no surprises, no wild card species, just the bottom program doing what it does this time of year.

Mackerel showed in good numbers around the Shoals early in the week, which is the real story if you're paying attention to bait rather than just species counts. Schools were working the surface around 6 a.m. off Star Island before the wind came up, and where you find mackerel that thick you generally find something interested in eating them. I picked up a few bluefish trolling small tinsel jigs behind the mackerel schools, nothing huge, 2 to 4 pounds, but scrappy and willing. The bigger blue fishing has been better closer to the harbors than out at the Shoals — Rye Harbor's outer breakwater and the mouth of the Piscataqua both had blues chasing bait on the last two hours of the incoming tide, and if you want steady action without the run offshore, that's where I'd put a rod.

Stripers are the interesting piece right now, and it's mostly a Hampton Harbor story. Snapper blues have been thick in the back channels behind Hampton Beach State Park for a couple weeks now, which is usually the tell that the bigger fish are close behind, and this week that started to bear out. I had reports of slot bass showing up on the flood tide pushing into the marsh creeks off Meadow Pond, feeding on mummichogs and small peanut bunker getting flushed out of the grass. Small white or chartreuse soft plastics on a light jighead, fished slow along the channel edges where the marsh drains into the main harbor, has been the go-to. Nothing blitzing, no top-water fireworks, but a real, catchable pattern on the last two hours of the incoming and first hour of the outgoing. Great Boars Head has produced a few fish from the surf too, mostly at first light on bucktails worked along the rock structure, but that bite has been more about timing than volume — you need to be there right as the tide turns, not an hour before or after.

Flounder are still around in the Piscataqua for the guys willing to anchor up and soak clam or sandworm on the bottom near the Route 1 bridge and down toward the Coast Guard station. It's not exciting fishing but it's honest fishing, and on a day when the wind's up and the Shoals run is a bad idea, it's a fine way to fill a cooler.

Looking ahead, the moon's building toward the full on the 28th, which should push more water through Hampton Harbor and strengthen that striper pattern in the marsh creeks — bigger tides usually mean more bait getting flushed and more fish willing to chase it into the shallows. If the mackerel stay parked around the Shoals, I'd expect the bluefish bite there to hold steady through the week, maybe build a little as more forage stacks up. Offshore, if I've got a calm morning window, I'm still starting at White Island on the slack and working the tide change — that's produced every week this month and I don't see a reason to abandon it. Worth checking wind before you commit to the run out there; it's a different ocean nine miles off Rye than it is inside the breakwater.
